write.desc: Series with nonnegative terms have monotone partial sums, so by completeness (the monotone convergence theorem) they converge exactly when their partial sums are bounded; the comparison, limit comparison and Cauchy condensation tests, the benchmark series they settle (p-series, logarithmic series, geometric comparison) and the convergence of decimal expansions all follow from this one fact, which is why they are studied together.

points.name: Bounded partial sums criterion
points.what: The learner can prove that a series with nonnegative terms converges if and only if its partial sums are bounded above, because the partial sums increase and the monotone convergence theorem applies, and can explain that this is where completeness enters (for example, the partial sums of the sum of 1/n! are bounded rationals whose limit e is not rational). Otherwise the series diverges to plus infinity; there is no oscillation.
outside: monotone convergence theorem for bounded monotone sequences
a series converges when its sequence of partial sums converges (definition of series convergence)

points.name: Comparison test
points.what: The learner can state and prove the comparison test: if 0 <= a_n <= b_n for all n beyond some N, then convergence of the sum of b_n gives convergence of the sum of a_n, and divergence of the sum of a_n gives divergence of the sum of b_n. They can use it in both directions, for example showing the sum of 1/sqrt(n) diverges by comparison with the harmonic series.
outside: changing or deleting finitely many terms does not affect convergence (tails of a series)

points.name: Cauchy condensation test
points.what: The learner can state and prove that for a nonincreasing sequence of nonnegative terms, the sum of a_n converges if and only if the sum of 2^k a_(2^k) converges, by grouping terms into blocks from 2^k to 2^(k+1)-1 and bounding each block above and below, and can explain why the monotonicity hypothesis is needed.

points.name: p-series by condensation
points.what: The learner can prove, without integrals, that the sum of 1/n^p converges exactly when p > 1: condensation turns it into a geometric series with ratio 2^(1-p), and for p <= 0 the term test applies. They recognise the harmonic series as the borderline case p = 1.
outside: geometric series converges exactly when the ratio has absolute value below 1

points.name: Logarithmic benchmark series
points.what: The learner can use condensation twice to show that the sum of 1/(n log n) diverges and that the sum of 1/(n (log n)^p) converges exactly when p > 1, and understands from this that there is no slowest divergent or fastest convergent series to compare against.
outside: basic properties of the logarithm (log of a power, monotonicity)

points.name: Writing the comparison inequality
points.what: The learner can turn an expression such as (n+1)/(n^3 - n + 5) into a correct, proved inequality against a benchmark, by enlarging the numerator and shrinking the denominator (or the reverse), valid for all n beyond a stated N. They avoid the classic mistakes: bounding above by a divergent series or below by a convergent one, which proves nothing, and inequalities that hold only in the wrong direction.
outside: manipulating inequalities between real numbers (order properties of the reals)

points.name: Limit comparison test
points.what: The learner can state and prove the limit comparison test: if a_n, b_n > 0 and a_n/b_n tends to a finite positive limit, the two series converge or diverge together (with the one-sided versions for limit 0 and limit infinity), by using the definition of the limit to get c b_n <= a_n <= C b_n eventually and then applying the comparison test. They can decide when limit comparison is easier than writing a direct inequality.
outside: epsilon-N definition of the limit of a sequence

points.name: Comparing with a geometric series
points.what: The learner can show convergence by proving a_n <= C r^n eventually with 0 <= r < 1, for instance when a_(n+1)/a_n <= r or a_n^(1/n) <= r for all large n, and sees this as the idea behind the ratio and root tests, which are stated and proved for absolute values in the next part. They can apply it to series such as the sum of n^2/2^n or n!/n^n.
outside: geometric series converges exactly when the ratio has absolute value below 1

points.name: Choosing a comparison series
points.what: Given a series of nonnegative terms, the learner can find its dominant behaviour (leading powers, logarithms growing slower than any power, exponentials faster than any power), pick a benchmark (geometric, p-series or logarithmic), decide between direct comparison, limit comparison and condensation, and write the justification as a short proof rather than a recipe.
outside: growth rates: log n is eventually smaller than any positive power of n, and n^k is eventually smaller than r^n for r > 1

points.name: Decimal expansions converge
points.what: The learner can prove that for any digits d_k in {0,...,9} the series of d_k/10^k converges, by comparison with the geometric series 9/10^k, to a number in [0,1], and can compute simple cases such as 0.999... = 1.
outside: sum of a geometric series (closed form)

points.name: Every number in [0,1] has a decimal expansion
points.what: The learner can prove that each x in [0,1] equals the sum of d_k/10^k for suitably chosen digits, by choosing each digit greedily (as the integer part of 10^k x minus 10 times the previous one) and showing the partial sums lie within 10^(-k) below x. They know that the expansion is unique except for numbers with two expansions, one ending in 0s and one ending in 9s.
outside: Archimedean property and existence of the integer part (floor) of a real number

where.title: Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed.)
where.detail: Section 2.4 (Monotone Convergence Theorem and a first look at infinite series, including the Cauchy condensation test) and Section 2.7 (Properties of infinite series, comparison test)

where.title: Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed.)
where.detail: Chapter 3, 'Series' and 'Series of nonnegative terms' (comparison test, Cauchy condensation, p-series and 1/(n (log n)^p))

where.title: Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis
where.detail: Section 3.7 (Introduction to infinite series, comparison and limit comparison tests); Section 2.5 for decimal representations of real numbers

where.title: Michael Spivak, Calculus
where.detail: Chapter 'Infinite Series' (comparison and limit comparison tests, condensation in the problems)
